title: Quorum concepts
description: Learn about quorum-based replication and consensus. Understand how to use read and write quorums to balance consistency, availability, and performance.

data.text: Quorum-based systems use majority voting to coordinate distributed operations. By requiring agreement from a subset of replicas, quorums provide a way to balance consistency, availability, and performance in replicated systems.
A quorum is the minimum number of votes required to make a decision. In distributed systems, quorums ensure that operations are acknowledged by enough replicas to guarantee certain properties.

items: Quorum = majority of replicas (more than half)
For N replicas, quorum = floor(N/2) + 1
Ensures that read and write quorums overlap
Prevents split-brain scenarios
Provides tunable consistency levels

data.text: The magic of quorums comes from the relationship between read quorum (R) and write quorum (W).
To guarantee that reads see the latest write: R + W > N

items: N = total number of replicas
W = number of replicas that must acknowledge a write
R = number of replicas that must respond to a read
When R + W > N, read and write quorums must overlap
This overlap ensures reads see the most recent write

data.title: Example
data.text: With 5 replicas (N=5): If W=3 and R=3, then R+W=6 > 5. Every read will see the latest write because the 3 replicas queried for the read must include at least 1 of the 3 that acknowledged the write.

items.title: Strong Consistency (R+W > N)
items.description: Example: N=3, W=2, R=2. Every read sees the latest write. Higher latency due to coordination, but guarantees consistency.

items.title: Fast Writes (W=1, R=N)
items.description: Writes are fast (single replica), reads query all replicas. Risk of stale data if the write replica fails before replication.

items.title: Fast Reads (W=N, R=1)
items.description: Writes are slow (all replicas), reads are fast (single replica). Good for read-heavy workloads with infrequent writes.

items.title: Balanced (W=⌈N/2⌉, R=⌈N/2⌉)
items.description: Both reads and writes require majority. Good balance between performance and consistency. N=3 means W=2, R=2.

data.text: Many distributed databases use quorum-based replication with tunable consistency levels.

items: Cassandra: Allows setting ANY, ONE, QUORUM, ALL for reads and writes
DynamoDB: Supports eventual and strong consistency modes
Couchbase: Configurable durability and replication levels
Riak: Tunable quorum settings per operation
MongoDB: Write concern and read concern levels
Higher quorum values = stronger consistency but higher latency
Lower quorum values = faster operations but risk of inconsistency
Asymmetric quorums (fast writes, slow reads) optimize for specific patterns
Network partitions can prevent achieving quorum, affecting availability
Quorum size affects fault tolerance—need enough replicas to maintain quorum during failures

data.title: Availability Consideration
data.text: With N replicas, you can tolerate up to (N - quorum) failures. For N=3 with quorum=2, you can only tolerate 1 failure. Design your replica count accordingly.

items: Read repair—detect inconsistencies during reads and fix them
Hinted handoff—temporarily store writes for failed replicas
Sloppy quorums—accept writes from any replicas during partitions
Consistent hashing—distribute data across many nodes efficiently
Weighted quorums—account for replica capacity or geography
